title: Review: Cell and nuclear division; Gene expression; Water potential; Reproduction

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Sexual reproduction
items.clue: Reproduction in which two gametes, produced by meiosis, fuse to form a zygote.

items.label: Reproductive strategy
items.clue: The pattern of investment a sex makes in producing gametes and in its offspring.

items.label: Histone
items.clue: One of a group of basic proteins around which DNA is wound in eukaryotic chromosomes.

items.label: Standard error
items.clue: A statistic that indicates how close the mean of a sample of repeats is likely to be to the true mean.

questions.stem: How is the DNA of a eukaryotic chromosome condensed before nuclear division?

options.text: The double helix itself twists ever more tightly, with no proteins involved, until the molecule is short enough to be seen.
The DNA is wound around histone proteins, and the fibre so formed is supercoiled into a much shorter, thicker structure.
The DNA is already packed as a condensed chromosome throughout the cycle; staining at division merely makes it visible.
The DNA is copied, and the two new copies pack tightly against each other to form the short, visible chromosome.

questions.stem: Which statement about the phases of mitosis in a human cell is correct?

options.text: In anaphase, the two chromosomes of each homologous pair are separated and moved to opposite poles.
In metaphase, the chromosomes line up at the equator while still enclosed within the nuclear envelope.
In prophase, each chromosome is replicated so that it consists of two chromatids by the end of the phase.
In anaphase, the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated and moved to opposite poles.

questions.stem: Two cells are seen in a stained micrograph of a root tip. Cell 1 has an intact nucleus in which no separate chromosomes can be distinguished. Cell 2 has no nuclear envelope, and its condensed chromosomes lie in a single line across the middle of the cell. Which identification is correct?

options.text: Cell 1 is in prophase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in prophase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in early anaphase.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly outlines the two rounds of segregation in meiosis?

options.text: In meiosis I the two chromosomes of each homologous pair separate; in meiosis II the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate.
In meiosis I the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated, and in meiosis II the homologous chromosomes of each pair are separated.
In meiosis I the homologous chromosomes are separated; the DNA is then replicated so that meiosis II can separate the new chromatids.
In meiosis I each chromosome is split into its maternal chromatid and its paternal chromatid, and meiosis II shares these between nuclei.

questions.stem: Which statement about crossing over is correct?

options.text: Sister chromatids of one chromosome exchange lengths of DNA, so that the two chromatids come to differ from each other.
The exchange of DNA alters the base sequence at the exchanged region, creating new alleles of the genes found there.
The exchange between chromatids decides which chromosome of each pair moves to each pole of the cell in anaphase I.
Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange lengths of DNA, producing new combinations of alleles.

questions.stem: Which statement about the tissue fluid that bathes the cells of a mammal is correct?

options.text: It is kept slightly hypotonic to the cytoplasm of the cells, so that they are kept fully hydrated by a steady inflow of water.
It is kept isotonic with the cytoplasm of the cells, so that they neither swell and burst nor shrink through net osmosis.
It is kept isotonic with the cytoplasm of the cells, so that no water molecules cross their membranes at all.
Its concentration does not need regulating, because cells that take in excess water become turgid and then stop.

questions.stem: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cell swells until it bursts, like an animal cell in pure water.
Solutes leave the cell into the pure water until the cell sap is as dilute as the water outside.
The cell pumps water in, using energy, until it is full and then it switches the pumping off.
Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid, its wall resisting further expansion.

questions.stem: What is the relative advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?

options.text: Its offspring carry new gene combinations, giving the variation needed for a changed environment.
Its offspring gain the particular features that a changed environment comes to require.
Its offspring are better adapted than the parent in every environment, so more of them survive.
Its offspring carry new alleles produced by meiosis, which asexual offspring cannot receive.

questions.stem: A student annotates a diagram of the male reproductive system. Which annotation is correct?

options.text: Urethra: carries urine only, because semen leaves through a separate duct in the penis.
Epididymis: stores sperm while they mature after their production in the testis.
Seminal vesicle: stores the sperm until they are required for ejaculation.
Testis: produces the semen that carries sperm along the duct to the urethra.

questions.explanation: Sperm are produced in the testis and pass into the epididymis, the coiled tube on its surface, where they mature and are stored until ejaculation.

questions.stem: Why is meiosis needed in a sexual life cycle?

options.text: Gametes could be produced by mitosis instead, because when two diploid gametes fuse the zygote they form is diploid like its parents.
Fertilization combines the chromosomes of two gametes, so the number must be halved beforehand to keep it constant across generations.
Each gamete must carry only half of the parent's genes, so that the offspring gets one half from each parent and no gene is duplicated.
Mitosis doubles the chromosome number each time a body cell divides, so meiosis is needed to bring the number back down again.

questions.stem: Red blood cells are placed in distilled water. What happens to them, and why?

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cells swell until their membranes are stretched taut, and then they remain turgid.
Water leaves by osmosis, because the cytoplasm is more concentrated than the distilled water, and the cells shrink.
Water leaves by osmosis, because distilled water is hypertonic to the cytoplasm, and the cells crenate.
Water enters by osmosis and the cells swell and burst, because no wall resists their expansion.

questions.stem: A student annotates a diagram of the female reproductive system. Which annotation is correct?

options.text: Uterus: the site of fertilization and, later, of implantation of the embryo.
Endometrium: the thick muscular wall of the uterus that contracts during childbirth.
Oviduct: the site of fertilization; it moves the egg towards the uterus.
Ovary: releases an egg into the oviduct on day 1 of each menstruation.

questions.explanation: The oviduct collects the egg released at ovulation, its cilia move the egg towards the uterus, and it is where sperm normally meet and fertilize the egg.

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic cell, a non-coding base sequence located 20 000 base pairs upstream of a gene is deleted. The promoter of the gene is intact, but transcription of the gene falls to a much lower rate. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The deleted sequence coded for a transcription factor, so less is now made
The deletion is unrelated, because a sequence so far away cannot affect the gene
The deleted sequence was part of the transcribed region, so a shorter mRNA is made
The deleted sequence was an enhancer to which activator proteins bound

questions.stem: A plant cell has a solute potential of −700 kPa and a pressure potential of +200 kPa. What is its water potential?

options.text: -500 kPa
-900 kPa
-700 kPa
+500 kPa

questions.explanation: ψw = ψs + ψp = (−700 kPa) + (+200 kPa) = −500 kPa. The positive pressure potential raises the water potential of the cell above its solute potential.
